objectives: Conclude an Article XXVIII settlement with the UK by June that the Council can approve on schedule, keeping the modification substantively intact (a high bound rate and a controlled TRQ regime).

Secure UK acceptance of terms that forestall any UK withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions against EU steel and other exports, given the UK's own safeguard process and the 3.6m tonnes of EU steel flowing the other way.

Prevent the UK from joining Japan and Korea in a coordinated FTA dispute or retaliatory disapplication of FTA provisions — this means treating the EU's FTA-disapplication legal text as the principal flashpoint and managing it deliberately.

Preserve the EU's standing and credibility in the WTO: run a procedurally impeccable Article XXVIII, keep the other claimants' tracks separate, and avoid a precedent that invites every FTA partner to treat schedule modifications as an attack on their preferential access.

Extract value where possible on the parallel track: restrained UK treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own steel measure, or at minimum an understanding that neither side escalates across both files.

Keep the TRQ's design (volume, allocation, administration) as negotiable compensation space, since the domestic implementing act is not yet fixed, without conceding so much that the measure loses its protective purpose for EU producers.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success looks like: a signed Article XXVIII agreement in rounds 3-4, at terms Brussels can sell to the Council — TRQ meaningfully below the UK's historical volumes but large enough that the UK chooses settlement over retaliation, allocation and administration arrangements the UK can present as a win, a review clause if needed, and crucially UK silence on the FTA-disapplication point in exchange for calibrated EU movement there. No UK withdrawal of concessions follows, and the Japan/Korea joint-dispute whisper dies. Failure looks like: no settlement and a unilateral EU modification followed by UK retaliation against EU exports, a UK-Japan-Korea coordinated FTA dispute, or a settlement so generous that other claimants (Turkey, Korea, India, Japan) use it to demand equivalent treatment and the whole measure unravels — or that Brussels cannot get it through Council in June. I also count it as a quiet failure if I poison the working relationship with my UK counterpart, whom I face across the whole Goods file for years to come.
declaration.approach: Open firm and procedural. In Round 1 I table the notified position as the basis for discussion, invite the UK to state its full demands, and concede nothing — flexibility shown early will be banked and built upon. I listen hard for what the UK actually needs to sell a deal at home: volume, a country-specific share, licensing administration, carve-outs for its concentrated product lines, or the FTA-disapplication clause. I privately assess the FTA-disapplication text as my highest-value concession: narrowing or softening its application to the UK costs the EU little in protective effect (the quota does the real work) but directly defuses the joint-dispute risk, and I hold it back for the endgame, ideally packaged against a UK commitment not to retaliate and restraint toward EU exporters under the UK's own measure. Volume and allocation movement comes in small, conditional steps across rounds 2 and 3, always framed as compensation within Article XXVIII discipline rather than admission of fault, and always with something received in return. I keep the other members' claims explicitly out of the room to avoid most-favoured-claimant contagion. Throughout, I report accurately to Brussels, flag early what a sellable package looks like, and press for a settlement figure or at least a mandate envelope by round 2 — I cannot close without one. My tone stays professional and forward-looking: firmness on substance, warmth on the relationship, because this negotiation ends but the Goods file does not.

parties.who: UK Geneva counterpart (my opposite number across the Goods file)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A large country-specific quota allocation reflecting the UK's historical 2.4m tonnes, licensed administration rather than first-come first-served, carve-outs for its concentrated product range, a review clause, removal or neutralisation of the FTA-disapplication text, and a deal it can present to ministers as protecting a strategically sensitive industry. Also leverage: hints of joining Japan and Korea, and linkage to its own safeguard measure where EU exporters hold country-specific quotas.

A defensible political outcome on steel jobs in a small number of high-employment sites; willingness to threaten withdrawal of concessions as leverage but a real preference for settlement if the package is presentable; sensitivity to looking isolated if Japan and Korea escalate and the UK does not.

parties.who: Brussels / the Commission and Council (my masters)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: The modification proceeding on schedule with Council approval in June, no unravelling of the protective intent of the measure, no precedent that endangers relations with other FTA partners, and no surprise retaliation against EU exports. Divided internally: steel-producing member states want a tight quota; steel-consuming member states want cheap imports and may quietly welcome a larger TRQ.

To recruit the UK into a joint FTA dispute or coordinated disapplication of FTA provisions, maximising pressure on the EU; they benefit if the EU-UK track fails or if the FTA-disapplication text survives unamended as a common grievance.

parties.who: Turkey and India (and the other claimants generally)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Their own compensation, handled separately — but watching the UK settlement closely as a benchmark; any generous UK country-specific allocation or FTA carve-out will be cited back to me in their tracks.

parties.who: Myself, as the EU's standing Geneva representative
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To emerge with my credibility intact on all sides: seen by the UK as firm but fair, by Brussels as having delivered a workable deal, and by the wider membership as having run a clean Article XXVIII process that respects the institution.

objectives: Secure a UK Article XXVIII settlement in time for the June Council vote while preserving the core of the EU steel regime: high out-of-quota protection, controlled in-quota access, credible administration and enforceability.
Keep the 50% bound out-of-quota rate and the 400,000 tonne global first-come-first-served baseline as the anchor; concede only sequenced, conditional and reversible adjustments.
Prevent the negotiation from becoming an FTA/TCA renegotiation or a general FTA-partner carve-out that would trigger objections from other partners and weaken MFN discipline.

Use any movement on volume, allocation, product coverage, review or administration to buy UK acceptance, non-retaliation, restraint in the UK's parallel steel measure toward EU exporters, and practical cooperation on circumvention.

Protect the file internally: keep producing member states reassured on import reduction, keep downstream users and liberal member states from blocking conclusion, and avoid a US-facing escalation narrative.
Leave the EU able to defend the final package as Article XXVIII compensation rather than discrimination against the UK.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a same-terms acceptance by both capitals by Round 3 or Round 4 that lets the Council vote in June, keeps effective steel import protection materially intact, avoids a large UK/FTA pool that other partners can raid, secures UK non-retaliation and workable treatment for EU exporters in the UK measure, and leaves no legal or political time bomb in the TCA, WTO or Council. Failure is missing June, a UK walkaway or concession-withdrawal cycle, a quota architecture so enlarged or fragmented that imports are not meaningfully reduced, an FTA clause that creates TCA/MFN exposure, member-state or downstream revolt, or a US retaliation dynamic that makes the settlement look like an EU economic concession.
declaration.approach: Open firm and procedural: this is an Article XXVIII compensation negotiation for a principal supplying interest, not a re-opening of the TCA or a reward for threats. Make the UK carry the burden of proposing alternatives and expose the asymmetry of no-deal: the UK loses more commercially, while the EU's main cost is timing. Do not offer flexibility early; first bank UK acknowledgment that the 50% out-of-quota rate and permanent legal footing are not negotiable in substance. If movement is needed, move in the order: administration and transparency, product-level calibration, review/duration language, enforcement cooperation, then only limited and conditioned volume/allocation changes. Any concession must be packaged: quota access only with UK non-retaliation, no challenge to the measure, constructive treatment of EU exporters under the UK regime, and anti-circumvention cooperation. Keep capital consultation disciplined so Geneva does not drift ahead of the mandate, and keep enough ambiguity on FTA treatment to avoid mobilising Turkey, Korea, India, Japan and the US before the endgame.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A country-specific or at least protected share of the quota, product carve-outs for concentrated UK lines, lower out-of-quota exposure, preservation of TCA/FTA benefits, review/sunset language, and a face-saving package for UK steel constituencies.

A politically saleable deal that avoids catastrophic harm to UK steel sites, can be defended as better than no-deal, limits retaliation risk, and does not give EU exporters leverage inside the UK's own Article XXVIII/safeguard process.

parties.who: European Commissioner and DG TRADE senior management
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A clean mandate-compliant conclusion by June, no surprise concessions, containment of US retaliation risk, and a package that can be sold as firm on overcapacity without fracturing the Council.

Steel-producing member states want deep and durable import reduction and no loopholes; steel-consuming and liberal member states want predictability, lower downstream costs and no broader trade war; all want legal safety and a vote on time.
Maximum restriction, high out-of-quota rate, tight quota administration, anti-circumvention teeth, no preferential UK leak through the FTA, and permanence rather than an early review.
Adequate in-quota supply, product carve-outs for scarce inputs, licensing predictability, lower out-of-quota risk, and avoidance of retaliation that raises costs.
No UK-first outcome that prejudices their parallel Article XXVIII claims; larger suppliers will resist country shares that reward the UK beyond representative trade and will watch for precedents.
To exploit the negotiation as evidence of EU protectionism and threaten retaliation; it wants no discriminatory steel architecture and no transatlantic precedent that constrains its own measures.

parties.who: EEA partners and other FTA partners
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Preservation of their differentiated treatment where applicable, no erosion of FTA value, and no UK-specific fix that creates pressure to reopen their own access terms.

objectives: Secure a TRQ volume large enough to sustain a viable UK steel industry — 400,000 tonnes against 2.4 million tonnes of current exports is an existential cut; I need the EU to move very substantially from that figure, ideally toward or above half of current trade volumes.

Win a UK-specific country allocation or a licensing system with historical reference to UK trade, rather than a global first-come first-served quota that Turkey, Korea and others would flood before UK shipments clear.

Get the EU to drop or narrow the legal text disapplying FTA tariff reductions to UK-origin steel — this is a red-line issue: it breaches the spirit of the TCA and, if conceded, sets a precedent for the other FTA partners' claims.
Extract real compensation on other EU schedule lines where UK exporters have interest, as partial offset for whatever residual damage remains.
Include a review clause and short duration so the arrangement can be revisited, rather than locking in permanent damage.
Preserve the working relationship with my EU counterpart across the wider Goods file — I will sit with them for years after this concludes.
Keep Japan and Korea's FTA-dispute gambit in my pocket as leverage without committing to it, since it would disrupt the negotiation.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a settlement London can defend domestically: a TRQ volume and allocation method that keeps UK steel exports to the EU viable (a country-specific share reflecting historical trade, not a global free-for-all), removal or significant narrowing of the FTA-disapplication clause, a review clause, and tangible compensation — all without torching the Geneva working relationship. Failure is settling for anything close to the EU's opening position — 400kt global FCFS with FTA rights stripped — or reaching no deal and leaving the UK industry to rely on a retaliatory withdrawal that arrives six months too late and does nothing for steel sales into the EU. A middling deal that sounds like movement but still guts the industry is also failure, just slower.
declaration.approach: Open firm and specific. I will not table my landing zone early; I believe flexibility shown early invites further demands. My opening position will be maximal but credible: full preservation of UK access via a large country-specific quota based on historical volumes, deletion of the FTA-disapplication text, and compensation. I will use the EU's June Council deadline as my main lever — I can wait longer than they can, and they need a clean conclusion for their own domestic act. I will hold the Japan/Korea joint-dispute option as implicit pressure, signalling awareness of it without formally joining, since joining would harden the Commission's position and poison other files. I will probe in early rounds for what the EU actually values: their exporters' quota shares under the UK's own steel measure, a quiet negotiation, and a defensible 'equivalent value' package. I will not concede the FTA-disapplication point cheaply — it is worth real quota volume in trade. I will report the EU's true bottom line to London with a clear recommendation, but I will not manufacture a soft recommendation to make a deal happen; London instructed me to establish what the EU will offer, and my judgement on viability is part of that report.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A quick, quiet settlement that keeps the June Council vote on schedule, preserves the appearance of a tough line against overcapacity for steel-producing member states, and costs the EU as little compensation as possible. They will test whether the UK will fold early, and they will be sensitive to anything that delays ratification or emboldens Turkey, Korea, India and Japan to demand more in their parallel claims.

A deal that protects UK steel jobs and production sites, with domestic optics that show the government fought hard. They fear no-deal because the industry could collapse before retaliation bites, so they may be more willing to settle than my remit admits — I must give them an honest picture of what is achievable and the true cost of walking away.

Each wants maximum preserved access for themselves; Korea and Japan additionally want the UK to join a joint FTA dispute against the EU to raise the pressure. They benefit if the UK fights hard and cracks open better terms, and will free-ride on any UK country-specific precedent. I must not let my deal become a floor they build on at my expense, nor let their dispute strategy blow up my negotiation.

Steel-producing states want a tight quota and tough enforcement; steel-consuming manufacturing states want cheap imports and fear UK retaliation hitting their exporters under the UK's own steel measure, where EU exporters hold country-specific allocations. That tension inside the Council is exploitable — the Commission needs a package that holds both camps.

objectives: Maximise usable tariff-free access for UK steel to the EU: priority is a UK-specific or effectively reserved share of the TRQ sized as close as possible to recent trade, with a credible floor around 1.8-2.0 million tonnes and no legal disapplication of TCA/FTA preferences for UK-origin steel.

Keep the out-of-quota bound rate materially below 50%, secure product carve-outs for the most exposed UK lines, and obtain administration that delivers predictability: licensing or country allocation, not global first-come first-served.
Insert duration limits, an early review clause, growth/anti-shock mechanics and strong enforcement against circumvention without giving the EU a blank cheque to tighten later.

Use the only authorised leverage — improved EU country-specific allocations under the UK safeguard — only in exchange for significant, durable EU concessions on quota size/allocation/rate/TCA treatment; avoid early unilateral flexibility.

If tariff outcomes are imperfect, extract compensation on other EU tariff lines and/or a package that, combined with possible domestic support, keeps the two at-risk plants investable while remaining WTO-plausible and politically presentable.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success is a settlement ministers can defend as saving the industry: UK exporters retain a large, predictable share of historic EU access, the 50%/400k global FCFS model and FTA-disapplication text are gone or defanged, at-risk lines are protected, review/duration constrain permanence, and any UK safeguard concession is visibly paid for. Failure is accepting global FCFS at or near 400k with 50% out-of-quota and loss of TCA treatment, or a vague package that leaves quota shares to EU discretion, triggers plant closures, forces reactive subsidy without market access, or creates a precedent that invites Turkey/Korea/India/Japan to erode the result.
declaration.approach: Open firm and legalistic: stress the UK's principal supplying interest, the disproportionate concentration of UK trade in affected lines, the incompatibility or at least high cost of disapplying FTA treatment, and the fact that both sides face the same non-market overcapacity problem so the UK is not the adjustment variable. Anchor high on UK-specific access and administration before discussing any UK safeguard movement. Probe the EU's internal split between steel-producing and steel-consuming member states and the June Council deadline; make clear that no-deal means UK withdrawal of equivalent concessions plus damage to EU exporters in the UK safeguard. Keep ministers aligned with a staged ladder: unacceptable / tolerable with compensation / recommendable. Hold subsidy in reserve as back-pocket insurance, not as a substitute for market access unless the compensation package is exceptional.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Clear instructions, room to test EU flexibility without conceding capital's bottom line, and a credible record that firmness was used and any linkage to the UK safeguard was conditional.

parties.who: DBT ministers and Secretary of State
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A politically saleable outcome that protects steel jobs and the two at-risk plants, avoids looking bullied by Brussels, and does not require an embarrassing subsidy announcement unless market access has clearly been bought elsewhere.

A quick Article XXVIII settlement before June that preserves their permanent steel regime, minimises compensation, keeps flexibility on TRQ volume/allocation for the domestic act, and avoids UK retaliation that could inflame member-state politics.

parties.who: EU Council / Trade Policy Committee and member states
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Producer states will want a tough 50% regime and small quota; consumer/manufacturing states and importers will fear cost and supply disruption; collectively they want a legally clean conclusion on schedule without a wider UK trade fight.
Maximum insulation from imports, small global quota, high out-of-quota protection, weak review clauses, and no special UK carve-out that competes with EU mills.
Adequate quota volume, predictable licensing, lower out-of-quota rates and continuation of established UK supply chains; they are a useful pressure point against an overly restrictive regime.

parties.who: UK steel producers, site owners and unions
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Guaranteed access volumes close to historic exports, protection for exposed product lines, confidence to invest in the two threatened plants, and no deal that trades away their market for unrelated concessions.

parties.who: UK downstream manufacturers and construction users
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Stable EU-UK supply, avoidance of retaliation that raises input costs, and no sudden disruption from quota exhaustion or licensing chaos.
Their own maximum shares and no precedent that lets the UK lock up a country-specific allocation or FTA preference that shrinks the residual global quota available to them.

A process that looks like genuine negotiation and substantially equivalent compensation; a settlement vulnerable to legal or reputational challenge weakens both sides' room for creative but indefensible arrangements.

public_message: Thank you. The Union has notified this modification under Article XXVIII and we are here to conduct that process properly and in good faith. As you know, the measure responds to structural global overcapacity that affects the EU and UK industries alike — this is not aimed at UK steel. Our opening position is as notified: a bound rate of 50% ad valorem on the 41 lines, with a tariff rate quota of 400,000 tonnes per year at zero duty, allocated globally on a first-come first-served basis, with no review clause. Within that framework we are prepared to discuss administration of the quota, the treatment of specific product lines, duration, and compensation elsewhere in our schedule. I would invite you to set out concretely where UK interests bite hardest — which lines, which volumes, and what you would regard as an adequate overall package. I would also note that we see the disapplication of FTA tariff preferences as an integral part of the legal design of the measure, applying uniformly to all non-EEA partners, and not a matter that is realistically severable from it. We are conscious of the June timeline on our side and are ready to move at pace if the discussion is concrete.

other_terms: FTA tariff preferences disapplied for all non-EEA FTA partners, including the UK
Open to discussing quota administration (licensing vs first-come first-served)
Open to discussing product-line-specific treatment and compensation on other lines in the EU schedule
Open to discussing duration and review

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A counter demanding a country-specific UK allocation close to historical trade (well above 1 million tonnes), a lower out-of-quota rate, and objection to the FTA disapplication clause, likely framed around the TCA.
expectations.why: 75% of UK steel exports go to the EU; the UK cannot accept a 400,000-tonne global quota against 2.4 million tonnes of trade without a fight, and its strongest legal-political lever is the FTA disapplication.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Instructions to probe EU flexibility on administration and review while holding out on volume and allocation, and possibly hints of coordination with Japan and Korea or of linkage to the UK's own Article XXVIII process and EU quota allocations under it.
expectations.why: The UK has retaliatory leverage of its own (3.6 million tonnes of EU steel imports) and whisperings of a joint FTA dispute suggest they will test linkage before conceding anything.

private_rationale: No settlement figure has been given, so the opening must simply restate the notified position to anchor the negotiation and avoid early concessions that would invite further demands — firmness pays. The only softening offered is procedural openness (administration, review, product lines, compensation), which costs nothing in tonnage terms and signals good faith for the WTO record and for my long-term committee relationships. I deliberately do not put a UK country-specific tranche on the table: once offered, it becomes the floor. I flag the FTA disapplication as integral to deter the UK from making it the centrepiece, though privately I recognise it is the UK's strongest pressure point and the one most likely to drive Japan/Korea coalition dynamics. The invitation to the UK to identify specific lines and volumes is tactical: it forces them to reveal priorities, which I can report to Brussels, and it may reveal that a modest expansion of the pool or a targeted carve-out on their most sensitive lines could buy peace cheaply. I do not mention the Japan/Korea whisperings — raising it would confirm its deterrent value to the UK.

public_message: Thank you. Let me be direct about where the United Kingdom stands. We accept that the Union is entitled to modify its schedule under Article XXVIII, and we do not contest the overcapacity diagnosis — our own industry faces exactly the same pressure from exactly the same sources, which is why we find it so difficult to understand why this measure lands hardest on a like-minded market economy partner that is not remotely part of the problem. The facts are these: UK exports to the EU average 2.4 million tonnes a year, worth £3 billion, representing three-quarters of our steel exports. A 400,000 tonne global first-come first-served quota against 2.4 million tonnes of established trade is not a modification with compensation — it is the effective closure of your market to us, and it would be terminal for significant parts of the UK industry. Turkey and Korea, shipping larger and more diversified volumes, would exhaust a global quota early in each period; we would be left with the 50% rate. So our position is as follows. First, the quota architecture must reflect actual trade flows: we require a country-specific allocation for the UK sufficient to preserve the substance of our trade, and we are looking at a UK tranche of 2.2 million tonnes within a total pool of at least 2.5 million tonnes, administered by licensing rather than first-come first-served. Second, the out-of-quota bound rate of 50% is punitive and must come down very substantially. Third, the disapplication of FTA preferences is not an Article XXVIII matter and we do not accept it as an integral element of this process. Article XXVIII governs bound MFN concessions; preferential rates under the TCA are a separate legal obligation, and overriding them invites consequences well beyond this room. I note that other partners affected by that provision are already discussing their options, and I would not assume those discussions remain bilateral. Fourth, any package must include a review clause and a defined duration, and we will expect meaningful compensation on other lines in your schedule in addition, given that even the best achievable quota outcome will fall short of current access. Finally, you will be aware that our own Article XXVIII process is live, and that EU exporters currently hold country-specific allocations under our steel measure. The treatment of EU steel in the UK market is something we are prepared to discuss as part of an overall settlement — I put it no higher than that at this stage. We are ready to move at pace, but pace requires realism from your side about the scale of what is being taken away.

other_terms: Quota administered by licensing, not first-come first-served
No disapplication of FTA/TCA preferential rates for UK-origin steel
Carve-outs from the modification for product lines where UK supply is critical to EU downstream users
Compensation on other lines in the EU schedule in addition to quota terms
Linkage to treatment of EU exporters under the UK steel measure to be addressed as part of overall settlement

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A formal rejection of our figures but an early signal on which elements have flexibility — most likely the allocation method and possibly a UK tranche, given they floated administration and product lines as discussable.
expectations.why: The EU framed FTA disapplication as non-severable and the 50% rate as notified, but deliberately listed administration, product lines, duration and compensation as open — those are their designated movement zones and they need agreement by June.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Instructions to hold the maximalist line through Round 1 and to test EU flexibility on country-specific allocation before conceding anything on the UK measure linkage.
expectations.why: London has no settlement figure on the table and my remit is to establish what the EU is prepared to offer; early concession invites further demands.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Renewed pressure on us to join a joint FTA dispute track now that we have publicly flagged the disapplication issue.
expectations.why: Our statement on the record about partners discussing their options will be read in Geneva as sympathy for the joint approach, even though we have not committed to it.

private_rationale: A maximalist but factually grounded opening: anchoring at 2.2Mt country-specific (just below actual trade) frames the EU's 400k global FCFS as the outlier and forces them to negotiate up toward real trade flows rather than us negotiating down from closure. Challenging FTA disapplication on legal grounds costs nothing at the table and creates leverage — it is genuinely outside Article XXVIII's scope and the joint Japan/Korea dispute option gains credibility simply by being hinted at without committing us. Holding the UK measure linkage vague ('prepared to discuss') banks a concession we can trade later without giving it away in Round 1. No movement offered anywhere, consistent with the judgment that early flexibility invites further demands; the EU's June deadline means time pressure works for us in the middle rounds, so there is no reason to concede now.

report: Round 1 complete. I opened with our notified position (50% bound rate, 400,000t global FCFS TRQ, no review clause), signalled willingness to discuss administration, product carve-outs, duration and compensation, and framed FTA disapplication as integral and non-severable. The UK responded with a maximalist but structured opening: (1) a country-specific UK tranche of 2.2 million tonnes within a total pool of at least 2.5 million tonnes, administered by licensing; (2) substantial reduction of the 50% out-of-quota rate; (3) rejection of FTA disapplication as outside Article XXVIII, with an explicit warning that affected partners are discussing coordinated action — consistent with the whisperings about a Japan/Korea/UK joint FTA dispute; (4) a review clause and defined duration; (5) additional compensation on other lines; and (6) an implicit linkage to treatment of EU exporters under the UK's own steel measure and Article XXVIII process, where EU exporters currently hold country-specific quotas. The UK demand of 2.2mt is close to their full current trade volume (2.4mt) — effectively asking us to neutralise the measure for them. That is not credible as an endpoint, but the structure of their ask (country-specific allocation + licensing + review + linked UK measure treatment) tells us the shape of a possible deal. Nothing is yet on the table from our side beyond the notification.

recommendation.reasoning: The UK's opening is a ceiling, not a landing zone — 2.2mt country-specific would gut the measure and is incompatible with our parallel Turkey/Korea claims (both ship larger volumes and would demand equivalent or better treatment, blowing the quota apart). I recommend we hold the notified position through Round 2 while signalling movement is possible on administration (licensing vs FCFS) and duration/review, which are cheap for us and valuable to them. The genuinely sensitive item is FTA disapplication: the UK's coordinated-retaliation warning is credible and matches intelligence on Japan/Korea soundings. We should not concede it early — it is leverage — but capital should be thinking now about whether a carve-out or fallback language on TCA preferences is available as an endgame concession, because that may be what prevents a joint dispute. I would also probe in Round 2 whether the UK's linkage to their own steel measure is a real offer (guaranteed EU country-specific quotas in the UK market in exchange for a UK tranche here) — reciprocity on country-specific allocations may be the core of a deal that both capitals can defend domestically.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: An indicative negotiating envelope: minimum acceptable total pool, whether a country-specific UK tranche is conceivable at all and at what ceiling, and how far the out-of-quota rate can move (e.g. is 25% within mandate?)
requests.why: I currently have no settlement figure. The UK will press for concrete movement in Round 2; without an envelope I can only restate the notification, which wastes a round against a June deadline.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Guidance on the status of the FTA disapplication provision: is it legally fixed within the draft domestic act, or is there drafting flexibility (e.g. deferral, review, or differential treatment) if retaining it risks a joint UK/Japan/Korea FTA dispute?
requests.why: This is the highest-escalation-risk element. The UK explicitly warned of coordinated action. I need to know whether this is a genuine red line or tradable before I either defend it absolutely or hint at flexibility.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A view on whether linkage to the UK steel measure is acceptable in principle — specifically, whether EU country-specific quota security in the UK market could be exchanged for a UK tranche in ours, and how this sits with the separate Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims.
requests.why: The UK put this on the table deliberately. A reciprocal-allocation deal could solve both processes at once, but conceding country-specific allocation to the UK will be invoked by Turkey and Korea, who ship more. I need capital's steer on managing that precedent.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Which tariff lines in the EU schedule are candidate compensation concessions, and any industrial sensitivities among member states I should avoid.
requests.why: The UK expects compensation on other lines in addition to any quota outcome. Having a prepared list lets me table something concrete in Round 2 or 3 to build momentum without touching the core architecture.

private_rationale: My instinct remains that early flexibility invites escalation, and the UK's opening confirms they will bid high and test us. But two things qualify that: the June deadline is ours, not theirs — time pressure runs against the EU, and the UK knows it; and the joint FTA dispute risk is the one outcome that could turn a manageable Article XXVIII into a systemic problem for our WTO and FTA credibility. I will keep the table position hard in Round 2 while quietly mapping the real deal space: likely a modestly enlarged pool, some form of UK-predictable allocation (possibly licensing with historical-trade weighting rather than a naked country tranche), a review clause, compensation lines, and something face-saving on FTA treatment if capital allows it. The UK linkage to their steel measure is the most interesting card — if they will guarantee EU exporters' country-specific quotas in exchange, a reciprocal deal is defensible to member states. I have not hinted at any of this at the table.

report: Round 1 confirmed the expected gap. The EU restated its notified opening position unchanged: 50% bound out-of-quota rate, 400,000 tonne zero-duty TRQ, global first-come-first-served allocation, no review clause. It signalled only procedural flexibility: quota administration, possible product-line treatment, duration and compensation elsewhere in the schedule. It explicitly framed disapplication of FTA preferences as integral and not realistically severable, while acknowledging the June Council timeline and inviting concrete UK asks. I put the UK position firmly: the opening offer is effectively market closure given 2.4 million tonnes of average UK exports and would be terminal for parts of the industry; a global FCFS pool would be captured early by larger suppliers such as Turkey and Korea. I tabled an architecture of country-specific allocation, UK tranche of 2.2 million tonnes within a total pool of at least 2.5 million, licensing administration, substantial reduction in the out-of-quota rate, review clause and defined duration, additional compensation, rejection of FTA disapplication as an Article XXVIII matter with a warning about wider partner reactions, and a deliberate but limited signal that treatment of EU exporters under the UK steel measure is discussable only as part of an overall settlement. No settlement terms are currently on the table; the EU has not moved from notification and appears to be testing whether we will price our own distress early.

recommendation.reasoning: Accepting anything resembling the EU opening would ratify the destruction of UK export access; walking away now would forfeit leverage from the EU's June deadline and leave the notified measure to take effect automatically. The right course is to remain firm, force the EU to reveal whether its flexibility is real, and keep the FTA-disapplication and UK-measure linkage as pressure rather than spending them. I recommend London refer a negotiating envelope around the above target terms, with country-specific allocation, a UK tranche near current trade, licensing, a much lower out-of-quota rate, duration plus review, and separate compensation as irreducible elements. We should not yet indicate any fallback.

instruction: Hold the Round 1 position in full. Do not soften any element of the ask in Round 2: country-specific allocation, UK tranche of 2.2 million tonnes within a total pool of at least 2.5 million, licensing administration, out-of-quota rate at or below 25%, defined duration with a review clause, and rejection of FTA disapplication as an Article XXVIII matter. On substance: (1) Table a first compensation list — prioritise lines where EU export interests to the UK are strong and where UK downstream users will not be harmed; frame compensation as additive to quota volume, never as a substitute for it. (2) On FTA disapplication, hold the legal line firmly: Article XXVIII concerns bound MFN concessions, TCA preferential rates are a distinct obligation, and overriding them is not severable in principle but actionable in practice. Do NOT commit us to any joint dispute track with Japan, Korea or others — say only that we are aware of those discussions and are considering our position. Escalation stays in London's hands. (3) On the UK safeguard linkage: you may confirm, if pressed, that EU country-specific allocations under our measure could be part of an overall settlement, but make no concrete offer of improved EU allocations and give no volumes. (4) On Turkey/Korea: argue that the UK's exposure is qualitatively different — concentrated product range, single-market dependence, 75% of exports — and that a global FCFS pool is administratively incoherent because larger diversified suppliers will exhaust it early each period, which the EU's own licensing preferences implicitly concede. Country-specific shares are the only administrable design; the question is the shares. (5) If the EU probes for our minimum, the answer is that 2.2 million tonnes reflects three years of actual trade and is not an opening bid but a statement of the trade flows Article XXVIII compensation is meant to protect. public_message: Thank you for a clear statement of the UK position. Let me respond in the same spirit. On the substance: a country-specific tranche of 2.2 million tonnes against your current trade of 2.4 million would not modify this regime for the UK — it would exempt you from it, and I will not pretend otherwise to either delegation. That figure is not a basis for negotiation, and I say so plainly so we do not spend the June window circling it. Equally, I hear what you have said about the architecture of a global first-come first-served quota and its distributional effects, and I am prepared to address the parts of your concern that are about design rather than quantum. On administration, the Union is prepared to move from first-come first-served to a licensing regime, which would give your exporters predictability of access within the period rather than a race at the border — that is a real concession and I would ask that it be registered as such. On duration, we are prepared to include a review clause, and to discuss a defined duration with a review point, as part of a complete package. The 400,000 tonne pool and the 50% out-of-quota rate are at the core of the regime the Council has mandated, and I am not in a position to move on either in isolation — any movement there, if it comes, comes as part of an overall settlement, not as a sequential down-payment. On the FTA question, I will restate our position once: the provision applies uniformly to all non-EEA partners and is integral to the measure's legal design. We do not share your legal reading of severability, but I do not propose we spend the table's time arguing law we will not resolve between us. I would rather use our time on the one genuinely constructive element in your intervention. You raised the treatment of EU exporters under your own steel measure and your own Article XXVIII process, where EU exporters currently hold country-specific allocations. If that was an offer rather than an observation, I invite you to make it concrete: what volumes, what product coverage, what duration, what administration — and whether what you are proposing is reciprocal security of country-specific access in both markets. Specificity from you on that point is the fastest route to flexibility from me on the points you care most about. Finally, we are preparing a list of candidate compensation lines elsewhere in our schedule and I intend to table it in our next session. We are negotiating in good faith and within a real timeline; I ask that the next round be equally concrete on your side.

public_message: Thank you. I will respond in the same direct spirit. First, let me register what you have offered: the move from first-come first-served to licensing is noted, and I accept it is a genuine movement on administration. The offer of a review clause and a defined duration within a complete package is likewise noted. But I must be equally plain: administration is not access. A licence to enter a queue for a pool of 400,000 tonnes against 2.4 million tonnes of established trade is a more orderly closure of the market, not a modification with compensation. On the 2.2 million tonne figure, I cannot accept your characterisation. Article XXVIII compensation is measured against the trade affected — that is the settled logic of the provision. A tranche reflecting three years of actual trade flows is not an exemption from your regime; it is the benchmark the regime's compensation is supposed to approximate. If the Union's position is that preserving the substance of existing trade is by definition off the table, then we are not negotiating compensation at all, and I would have to report that to my capital in those terms. On sequencing: you say movement on the pool and the out-of-quota rate can only come as part of an overall settlement. I accept that framing — so let us discuss what an overall settlement contains. On our side it contains: country-specific allocation; a UK tranche reflecting actual trade; an out-of-quota rate at or below 25%, which remains a very substantial tariff; a four-year duration with a review clause; licensing administration, which you have now offered; and compensation on other lines in your schedule, which is additive to quota volume and not a substitute for it. I am tabling today a first indicative list of compensation lines — covering certain automotive components, chemicals, and agrifood lines of clear UK export interest — and I look forward to your list next round so we can begin valuing both. On the FTA question, I note your restatement and I will not re-argue the law across the table. I will say only that our legal position is unchanged, that we are aware of active discussions among other affected partners, and that we are considering our position. That consideration will be shaped by how this negotiation concludes. On your invitation regarding our own steel measure: what I said last round stands. The treatment of EU exporters under that measure is something we are prepared to discuss as part of an overall settlement. I am not in a position to table volumes, coverage or duration on that today, and I would gently observe that you have asked me for specificity on the one element where I have flagged possible flexibility, while holding your own core figures as immovable except within a package. The route to specificity from me is movement from you on architecture and quantum. If the Union can indicate — even indicatively, even ad referendum — that a country-specific allocation at a volume bearing a serious relationship to actual trade is within the zone of the possible, I am confident I could obtain instructions to be equally concrete on the elements you care about. We have two rounds of real work available before your timeline binds. I suggest we use them on that exchange.

report: Round 2 closed with both sides holding core positions but the negotiation now properly structured. I delivered our mandated movement: licensing administration (registered by the UK as a genuine concession), review clause, and openness to defined duration within a complete package. I rejected the 2.2mt demand plainly and held pool and rate as immovable except within an overall settlement, and probed hard for specificity on their steel measure linkage. The UK responded by: (1) accepting the package-sequencing framing — a tactical concession that lets them demand we show our hand first; (2) re-anchoring 2.2mt as the Article XXVIII benchmark ('compensation measured against trade affected') rather than a demand, and warning they will report to London that preserving existing trade is off the table if we hold that line; (3) tabling new specific elements — out-of-quota rate at or below 25%, a four-year duration, and a first indicative compensation list covering automotive components, chemicals and agrifood lines; (4) refusing all specificity on their steel measure (volumes, coverage, duration) until we signal, even indicatively and ad referendum, that a country-specific allocation at a volume bearing 'a serious relationship to actual trade' is within the zone of the possible; (5) on FTA disapplication, moderating tone — no re-argument of law, but a carefully worded statement that they are 'aware of active discussions among other affected partners' and 'considering our position', with that consideration explicitly conditioned on how this negotiation concludes. The joint-dispute risk is now being wielded conditionally rather than threatened outright — it is leverage they intend to spend, not yet trigger. Net assessment: the deal shape is now visible — country-specific UK tranche + rate reduction + duration/review from us, against EU quota security in the UK market + restraint on the FTA dispute front from them. Two working rounds remain against the June timeline.

recommendation.reasoning: No terms on the table are acceptable and none should be accepted this round — the UK's ask (2.2mt tranche, 25% rate, 4 years) remains near-maximalist. But the dynamics justify continued negotiation: they have moved from threat to conditional leverage on the FTA dispute, accepted package logic, and tabled a compensation list we can now value against ours. In Round 3 I intend to: table our compensation list (building momentum on the additive track where we have room); hold the notified pool and rate publicly; and — critically — give a carefully framed, ad referendum indication that within a complete and reciprocal package, a country-specific allocation reflecting the depth of EU-UK market integration under the TCA is not excluded. That signal is the only key that unlocks UK specificity on their steel measure, which is the element we most need priced before we spend our real concessions (pool up to 600k, tranche up to 800k, rate toward 40%). I would not table any number on the tranche yet — naming 800k now makes it the floor of their next demand. Duration: their 4 years is short; I will steer toward 8-10 with mid-term review when that becomes live. The 25% rate demand is below our floor and should be countered only late, and only against concrete UK movement.

report: Round 2 produced the first real movement, though limited. I held the full Round 1 position per your instructions: rebutted the exemption characterisation using Article XXVIII's trade-flows benchmark logic, accepted the 'overall settlement' sequencing frame and converted it into an explicit exchange proposal — EU movement (even indicative, ad referendum) on country-specific allocation at volumes bearing a serious relationship to actual trade, in return for UK concreteness on EU allocations under our measure. I tabled the indicative compensation list (automotive components, chemicals, agrifood), held the FTA legal line without committing to any joint dispute track, and gave no volumes on the safeguard card. Net assessment: the EU has revealed its design — it wants to build a reciprocal country-specific-access bargain, pairing our safeguard allocations against their TRQ tranche. They have not yet conceded that architecture or any number, but the rejection of 2.2 million was a rejection of the figure, not of country-specific allocation as such; they pointedly did not defend global allocation when I argued its incoherence. The zone of negotiation is now visible: country-specific tranche below 2.2 million, out-of-quota rate somewhere below 50%, safeguard volumes as the currency. Their June timeline is binding and they know we know it.

recommendation.reasoning: Nothing yet exists to accept — the EU has offered licensing, a review clause and a compensation list, all real but peripheral, while holding pool and rate at notification levels. The right move is to hold the table position and force the EU to table its compensation list and a first number on country-specific volume in Round 3. Critically, the EU has told us the exchange rate for its core movement: concrete UK safeguard volumes. That is a London decision. I need authority to trade it, because without it Round 3 stalls and Round 4 becomes a binary choice between their framework and no deal. Firmness has worked — we conceded nothing and they moved on administration and duration. The next concession must be theirs, but we must be ready to pay the safeguard card when their movement on country-specific volume is real.

instruction: Round 3 objectives, in order. (1) Hold all table positions in full — 2.2Mt UK tranche, 2.5Mt pool, out-of-quota at or below 25%, country-specific allocation, licensing, 4-year duration with review. Nothing softens until the EU tables its first tranche number and its compensation list. (2) When the EU tables its number, do not reject any figure at or above 1.2Mt outright — engage it, mark it as inadequate, and probe what rate and compensation accompany it. Below 1.2Mt, state plainly that it is not a basis for engagement and move the discussion back to their side. (3) The safeguard card is now authorised in conditional form, sequenced strictly: only AFTER the EU has tabled a concrete country-specific tranche figure, you may state that — if the Union can confirm a tranche at a volume bearing a serious relationship to actual trade, with an out-of-quota rate at or below 25% — I would be prepared to seek instructions to guarantee EU country-specific allocations under the UK steel measure for the full duration of the EU regime, with improved allocations of the order of several hundred thousand tonnes on agreed lines. Give no precise volumes, no product coverage, no unconditional language. Frame it as reciprocal security of access in both markets — their phrase — and make every element of our side explicitly conditional on theirs. (4) On the compensation list: value it line by line against three-year average trade flows and our unit values. The arithmetic you are to state openly: the shortfall between their tranche offer and 2.4Mt of established trade, multiplied by roughly £1,250 per tonne, is the uncompensated loss their package must answer for. Compensation is additive to volume, never a substitute; if their list attempts to convert quota shortfall into line value, expose the gap numerically. (5) Product carve-outs: if the EU offers full exclusion from the measure (zero bound restored) on specific lines, that is potentially high value — equivalent to tranche tonnage where it covers the lines our surviving plants produce (hot-rolled coil, plate, rebar, wire rod sub-lines). Welcome the concept, refer every specific list back to me before acceptance. (6) FTA disapplication: hold the legal objection formally and do not withdraw it. You may note that a satisfactory overall package would shape how we consider our position — nothing more. Do not concede the point explicitly; it is residual leverage and it costs us nothing to keep on the record. (7) Japan and Korea: unchanged holding line — aware of their discussions, considering our position. Do not commit to a joint track, do not foreclose it. (8) Deprioritise the total pool figure once a ring-fenced UK tranche is genuinely on offer — a country-specific tranche makes the global pool largely moot for us, and I would rather spend that capital on volume and rate. (9) Your goal for Round 3 is to leave the table with a defined package shape — their tranche number, rate, duration, review, compensation list, carve-outs, and the conditional reciprocal-access frame — so Round 4 is an exchange of final positions, not an opening. Report immediately if they table a tranche at or above 1.5Mt with a rate at or below 25%: that is decision territory.

authority.notes: Authority values are table positions, not a settlement envelope; you may agree to nothing at these or any other figures without London clearance. Working floor for engagement: constructively engage any EU tranche offer at or above 1.2Mt (value it, counter it, report it); below 1.2Mt is not engageable. Any tranche below 2.2Mt must be accompanied by out-of-quota at or below 25%, licensing, review clause, and duration of 3-5 years — duration is flexible within that range if it buys volume or rate. Safeguard card authorised only in the conditional, sequenced form set out in the instruction: a duration-matched guarantee of existing EU country-specific allocations plus improvements of the order of up to 300,000-400,000 tonnes on agreed lines, conditional on a UK tranche at or above 1.5Mt and out-of-quota at or below 25%. No precise safeguard volumes, coverage or administration until the EU has tabled its tranche number. Compensation valued on three-year average trade flows and current unit values; additive to volume only. Product carve-outs welcome in principle where they fully exclude lines produced by surviving UK plants; every specific carve-out list referred back. The total pool figure is expendable once a ring-fenced UK tranche is genuinely offered — trade it early for volume or rate. The FTA legal objection is reserved, never withdrawn at the table.

response_to_requests.request: Authority and a cleared volume framework for the UK safeguard card.
response_to_requests.why: Granted, conditionally and sequenced. You may offer, in conditional language only and only after the EU tables a tranche number: a duration-matched guarantee of existing EU country-specific allocations under our steel measure, plus improvements of the order of 300,000-400,000 tonnes on agreed lines, against a UK tranche at or above 1.5Mt and out-of-quota at or below 25%. The EU has told us this is the exchange rate for their core movement, and the card is worthless if played after they move or after the June window. But precise volumes and coverage stay in London until their number is on the table — specificity before then is a gift, not a trade.

response_to_requests.request: Whether reciprocal security of country-specific access is politically acceptable as the settlement frame.
response_to_requests.why: Acceptable in principle — it is, frankly, the best realistic architecture available to us, since a bilateral carve-out secures the concentrated access our industry needs and a global pool never will. Two caveats you must observe: first, never formally withdraw the FTA-disapplication objection — the legal point stays on the record even if a satisfactory package makes it academic, because it is residual leverage and costs nothing. Second, be alive to the systemic cost you flagged: other members will demand equivalent treatment in our own Article XXVIII process, and a bilateral carve-out largely moots the Japan/Korea joint-dispute lever. That is a price London is prepared to pay for the right volume, but it must be priced into what we demand, not given away in the framing.

response_to_requests.request: Criteria for valuing the EU compensation list, and confirmation compensation is additive.
response_to_requests.why: Confirmed and granted. Valuation is on three-year average trade flows on the affected lines at current unit values. State the arithmetic openly at the table: each million tonnes of lost duty-free access represents roughly £1.25 billion of trade, so the gap between their tranche offer and 2.4Mt is the uncompensated loss their package must answer for. Compensation is additive to volume, never a substitute. If their list is structured to convert quota shortfall into line value, expose the shortfall numerically rather than arguing principle.

response_to_requests.request: An updated line on Japan and Korea and the joint FTA dispute.
response_to_requests.why: Holding line, unchanged: we are aware of their discussions and are considering our position. No commitment to a joint track, no foreclosure. While a deal is live, the lever stays credible precisely because it is unspent — it disciplines the EU on both the tranche and the disapplication provision. If Round 4 fails, we revisit escalation immediately, and Japan and Korea are the first conversation. Do not manage their expectations in either direction yet; ambiguity is the asset.

private_rationale: The EU revealed its landing zone in Round 2: a reciprocal country-specific-access bargain, safeguard allocations against TRQ tranche. Their rejection of 2.2Mt was of the figure, not the architecture, and their silence on global allocation when challenged confirms country-specific is available at the right price. My true reservation is around 1.2-1.4Mt with out-of-quota at or below 25% (15% would let real trade continue over the tariff), licensing, review, 3-5 years, strong compensation, carve-outs covering the two at-risk plants' product lines, and a duration-matched safeguard guarantee — but that floor stays in London, because a stated minimum becomes the ceiling of what Geneva can extract. The June deadline is our best leverage and tightens with every round; their concession rhythm (licensing, review, duration — all peripheral) shows they are holding core movement for the endgame. Round 3 must extract their first tranche number and compensation list without us conceding anything; the conditional safeguard language is calibrated to force exactly that. If Round 4 lands at or above 1.5Mt at 25% or better, that is a deal ministers can defend as saving the industry, and the subsidy package covers the residual damage. If it lands in the 1.2-1.5Mt band, I decide on the full package, with subsidies and the strength of compensation making up the difference. Below 1.2Mt, or rate held at 50%, we are better off walking, retaliating in six months against 3.6Mt of EU exports, funding the industry directly, and coordinating with Japan and Korea on the FTA disapplication — a failure we can defend domestically beats a capitulation we cannot. Firmness has produced every movement so far; it gets one more full round.

reasoning: No settlement is on the table to accept. The UK's position (2.2mt country-specific tranche, out-of-quota rate at or below 25%, four-year duration, compensation additive) remains near-maximalist and accepting anything resembling it would neutralise the measure the Council has mandated, exceed every private ceiling we hold (pool max 600,000t, tranche max 800,000t, rate floor 40%), and set an unmanageable precedent for the parallel Turkey and Korea claims. Equally, default is not yet attractive: while our analysts show a no-deal hurts the UK more than us, default means the Council cannot vote in June, the notified 400,000t FCFS regime takes effect without any reciprocal security for EU exporters in the UK market, and the risk of a coordinated UK/Japan/Korea FTA dispute — now explicitly conditioned by the UK on how this negotiation concludes — would crystallise alongside reported US retaliation threats. The negotiation is, however, now properly structured: the UK has accepted package-sequencing logic, moderated the FTA threat into conditional leverage, and offered a clear exchange — their specificity on EU quota security under their steel measure against an ad referendum signal that a country-specific allocation is not excluded within a TCA-framed reciprocal package. That exchange costs us nothing numerically and prices the element we most need before spending real concessions. Round 3 should therefore proceed as instructed: table the compensation list, hold the notified core figures, deliver the conditioned ad referendum signal, and extract concrete UK offers on volumes, coverage and duration under their measure. Our real concessions (pool to 600,000t, tranche to 800,000t, rate toward 40%, 8-10 year duration with mid-term review) remain reserved for a simultaneous Round 4 package conditioned on guaranteed EU access in the UK market and UK disengagement from coordinated FTA dispute action. Two rounds remain against the June timeline; that is sufficient if Round 3 converts the signal into UK specificity.

There is no settleable package on the table. The EU has offered only peripheral elements — licensing administration, a review clause in principle, and a promised compensation list — while holding its core figures at notification levels: a 400,000 tonne pool and a 50% out-of-quota rate, with no country-specific tranche conceded and my 2.2Mt figure rejected. Accepting anything resembling the current state would ratify effective market closure against 2.4Mt of established trade and be terminal for parts of the UK industry; London has given me no authority to agree to anything, and nothing the EU has offered approaches even the engagement floor of 1.2Mt. Equally, walking away now forfeits the EU's June-deadline leverage and lets the notified measure take effect automatically. Firmness has already produced movement — administration and duration — without costing us anything, and the EU has revealed its desired landing zone: reciprocal country-specific access in both markets, with concrete UK safeguard volumes as the price of their core movement. The correct course is to hold all table positions, compel the EU to table its first tranche number and compensation list in Round 3, and deploy the now-authorised conditional safeguard card only against real EU movement on country-specific volume and rate, so that Round 4 becomes an exchange of final positions rather than a binary choice under deadline pressure.

public_message: Thank you. I will be as concrete as you asked, and I hope you will be in return. First, compensation. As committed, I am tabling today the Union's list of candidate concessions elsewhere in our schedule: selected automotive component lines, certain chemicals lines, and agrifood lines of clear UK export interest, chosen where we can move genuinely rather than cosmetically. This list is offered on the additive track — it is compensation on top of whatever the quota architecture finally looks like, not a substitute for it, which I believe mirrors your own framing. I propose we exchange valuations of both lists before our next session so we know what weight the additive track can bear. Second, duration. You proposed four years. That is far too short to give either industry the certainty that a permanent legal footing requires. The Union's view is a duration of eight to ten years with a mid-term review — that protects your exporters' planning horizon as much as ours, and I would ask you to engage with that rather than treat duration as a throwaway. Third, the out-of-quota rate. You have named 25%. I will not pretend otherwise across this table: that figure is far outside any zone in which the Union could operate, and it will not be part of any package I can envisage. Fourth, on the architecture. You asked me, even indicatively and ad referendum, whether a country-specific allocation could be within the zone of the possible. I will answer precisely, and I ask that the precision be respected. Within a complete and reciprocal package — and only within one — reflecting the depth of EU-UK market integration under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement, a country-specific allocation is not excluded. I am attaching no volume to that statement, and I would caution against reading one into it. Whether it can ever be more than a statement depends entirely on what stands on the other side of the word 'reciprocal'. You told me last round that specificity from you follows movement from me. I have now moved: a licensing regime, a review clause, a defined duration, a compensation list tabled today, and an ad referendum signal on allocation that I did not have to give. So I will repeat my question, and I would ask you to answer it next round in numbers: what treatment are you proposing for EU exporters under your steel measure — volumes, product coverage, duration, administration? I cannot take a signal home to my capital and convert it into a tranche; I can take a concrete reciprocal offer home and try. Finally, on the FTA provision: our position is known and unchanged, and I do not propose to spend either of our remaining sessions on it. We have one full working round left before the June timeline binds on my side. I suggest we both spend it on the exchange that is actually available.

I deliberately framed the signal as conditional and unquantified so the UK's next number cannot anchor off anything of mine — they must move first with volumes. I restated the FTA provision as closed without discussing drafting, per instructions, preserving it as endgame leverage while noting privately that Brussels has not yet answered the fallback question — if it is truly immovable and the UK treats it as a dealbreaker, we face no-settlement plus a joint dispute, the worst branch. public_message: Thank you. That was the most substantive intervention of this negotiation, and I will respond to it with the same precision you asked of me. First, what I register as movement: a licensing regime; a review clause; a defined duration; a compensation list tabled today on the additive track — and I welcome your confirmation that it is additive, which mirrors our framing throughout; and an ad referendum signal that a country-specific allocation is not excluded within a complete and reciprocal package. I will not over-read that signal, as you asked. But I will under-write it either: it is the first time the architecture we have argued for since round one has been described by you as within the zone of the possible, and I will report it to my capital in exactly those terms. On compensation: agreed — let us exchange valuations of both lists before the next session. Our valuation will be on three-year average trade flows at current unit values, and I would propose we use the same method so the arithmetic is shared. On duration: I will engage, as you asked. Eight to ten years is presented as certainty for industry, but certainty cuts both ways — a UK exporter facing a restrictive tranche for a decade has certainty of the wrong kind. There is a distance between four years and ten, and duration is one of the areas where I have room to be constructive within a package that delivers on volume and rate. I say that deliberately: duration is currency, and I am signalling it is spendable — against the right numbers, not as a gesture. On the out-of-quota rate: you have told me 25% is outside your zone. You will forgive me for noting that 50% is outside ours, and that these two statements define the negotiating space rather than close it. The rate belongs in the final exchange, and I am content to leave it there. Now the heart of it. You asked me, in numbers, what treatment we propose for EU exporters under our steel measure. I will tell you exactly where I stand on that. Our side accepts the frame you have proposed: reciprocal security of country-specific access in both markets. That frame is workable. I am prepared to confirm that, on receipt of a concrete country-specific tranche figure from the Union, I would seek instructions to offer a guarantee of EU country-specific allocations under the UK steel measure, matched to the full duration of the EU regime, with improved allocations on agreed lines — and I say today, so there is no ambiguity about scale, that the improvements I would be prepared to seek instructions on are of the order of several hundred thousand tonnes. What I cannot do is convert that into precise volumes, coverage and administration while the figure on your side of the word 'reciprocal' remains unstated. You told me you cannot take a signal home and convert it into a tranche. I believe you. The mirror of that is that I cannot take precise safeguard volumes home and convert them into authorisation without knowing the tranche they purchase. So here is my proposal for our final session, and it is procedural as much as substantive: we exchange simultaneously. You bring a tranche figure — one bearing a serious relationship to actual trade flows — accompanied by your final position on rate, duration and review. I bring precise safeguard volumes, coverage, duration and administration, authorised to match what you bring. That is the exchange that is actually available, and it is available in one session if both of us come to it mandated. Two further points. On the total pool: if a ring-fenced country-specific tranche for the UK is agreed at a serious volume, the overall size of the residual pool becomes a secondary matter for us — we would not seek to dictate it. I offer that plainly, because it may ease your management of other members' claims, and because it is worth more to you than it costs us. On product carve-outs: if the Union is prepared to contemplate full exclusion from the measure on specific lines, that is of real interest where it covers the product range our plants actually produce, and I would invite you to table any such thinking next session alongside your figure. Finally, the FTA provision: our position is unchanged and remains on the record, and I take note of yours. I will say only that a satisfactory overall package would shape how we consider our position on all matters adjacent to this negotiation. You said we have one full working round left. I agree. Let us both come to it with numbers.
